questions.question: A postoperative client who received an IV opioid is difficult to arouse and has shallow respirations at 7/min while oxygen saturation is 95% on supplemental oxygen. What is the priority action?
choices: Stop opioid delivery, summon help, and support airway and ventilation
Document adequate oxygenation and allow the client to sleep
Give the next opioid dose because pain may cause shallow breathing
Remove supplemental oxygen and reassess in one hour
questions.explanation: Supplemental oxygen can preserve saturation despite dangerous hypoventilation. Stop opioid exposure, activate rescue, support ventilation, and prepare naloxone per protocol.

questions.question: A client begins breathing adequately after naloxone for an opioid overdose. Which action is most important next?
choices: Continue close monitoring for recurrent sedation and respiratory depression
Discharge immediately because naloxone permanently removes the opioid
Give a sedative to prevent withdrawal
Restart the opioid at the previous dose
questions.explanation: Naloxone may have a shorter duration than the opioid. Respiratory depression can recur, so continued monitoring and repeat dosing readiness are essential.

questions.question: A client takes scheduled acetaminophen, an opioid-acetaminophen combination, and an over-the-counter cold medicine labeled APAP. What is the nurse's best interpretation?
choices: All sources must be added to determine the 24-hour acetaminophen total
Only the scheduled tablets count toward the daily total
APAP is an NSAID and does not contain acetaminophen
Combination products cannot cause acetaminophen toxicity
questions.explanation: APAP is an abbreviation for acetaminophen. Every prescription and OTC source contributes to the same total and can cause severe liver injury if duplicated.

questions.question: Which client requires the greatest caution before receiving an NSAID?
choices: An older adult with chronic kidney disease, prior GI bleeding, and anticoagulant therapy
A young adult using a cold pack for an ankle sprain
An adult with an intact skin barrier using relaxation breathing
A client whose pain improves with repositioning
questions.explanation: Kidney disease, prior GI bleeding, older age, and anticoagulation substantially increase NSAID-related renal and bleeding risk.

questions.question: The family member of a sleeping client receiving PCA says, 'I press the button when the client looks uncomfortable.' What should the nurse do?
choices: Stop proxy dosing and teach that only the alert client may press the PCA button
Encourage the family member to press it every lockout interval
Increase the demand dose without an order
Disable respiratory monitoring so alarms do not disturb sleep
questions.explanation: Only the client presses the PCA button. Sedation naturally limits requests; proxy dosing bypasses this safeguard and can cause overdose.

questions.question: A client wearing a transdermal fentanyl patch places a heating pad directly over it. What should the nurse do first?
choices: Remove the heat source and assess for sedation and respiratory depression
Cover both with a blanket to stabilize absorption
Cut the patch in half to reduce the dose
Apply a second patch to another site
questions.explanation: External heat can increase fentanyl absorption and overdose risk. Remove the heat and immediately assess ventilation and level of consciousness.

questions.question: A client cannot swallow an extended-release opioid tablet. Which plan is safest?
choices: Hold it and request an appropriate alternative formulation
Crush it and mix it with applesauce
Chew it slowly with water
Dissolve it and give the entire dose rapidly
questions.explanation: Crushing, chewing, or dissolving an extended-release product can cause dose dumping. The nurse should hold it and obtain a suitable prescribed alternative.

questions.question: Which newly reported medication use most increases concern before an opioid dose?
choices: A benzodiazepine taken with alcohol
A topical moisturizer
A saline nasal spray
A daily multivitamin
questions.explanation: Opioids combined with benzodiazepines and alcohol can produce profound sedation and life-threatening respiratory depression.

questions.question: Which plan best addresses a predictable effect of continuing opioid therapy?
choices: Begin the prescribed bowel-prevention plan and monitor bowel function
Wait for fecal impaction before treating constipation
Restrict all fluids regardless of clinical condition
Use naloxone every day to prevent constipation
questions.explanation: Opioid constipation commonly persists. Prevention and monitoring are safer than waiting for severe constipation or impaction.

questions.question: A client taking a prescribed opioid regularly develops withdrawal when doses are abruptly stopped but has no impaired control, craving, or continued use despite harm. Which interpretation is best?
choices: Physical dependence can occur without opioid use disorder
Withdrawal alone proves opioid use disorder
The client is fabricating symptoms
Tolerance and addiction are identical
questions.explanation: Physical dependence is an expected physiologic adaptation in some clients and does not by itself establish opioid use disorder, which requires a broader clinical pattern.
